content.thinking:
I need to write this postmortem without inserting any numbers myself, using placeholders like {duration} and {began} instead. I should avoid stating specific latency figures since those are only candidate estimates, not confirmed data from the record.

For the causal chain, I'm building three steps: the symptom with metric placeholders citing the relevant tickets, the trigger being the monthly-spend-feature flag rollout citing its change records, and the suspected code-level cause (direct purchase history lookups instead of cache) as an unconfirmed hypothesis supported by recovery timing after the flag revert. I'm also flagging a discrepancy between the candidate's claimed change timestamp and what the records actually show—zero production changes logged versus one flag change at a different time—which needs to be noted as an assumption rather than fact.

Recovery timing is ambiguous too: metrics show recovery around the same time as the revert, so it's unclear whether the revert actually caused recovery or if it was coincidental self-resolution, and I need to caveat that honestly rather than overclaim causation. For contributing factors, I'm identifying the missing pre-rollout latency check and the alert firing only after impact had already ended, then mapping these to concrete action items (staged rollout with guardrails, correlating flag changes with alerts, load testing the feature path) labeled as AI-3, AI-4 etc. without inventing specific numeric figures like exact minute counts.

I'm finalizing three new action items: AI-3 for gating the rollout behind a staged percentage ramp with automatic latency guards, AI-4 for faster tail-latency paging plus feeding flag changes into the change-event feed, keeping AI-2 as the existing fix for the cache gap. Now I'll move on to writing the lessons-learned section.

action_items.item: Roll out monthly-spend-feature, and flags like it, in stages (a small percentage first) with an automatic hold or rollback when tail latency on the affected page rises. Re-enable it only after the fix is merged and checked under realistic load.

Fix the HighLatency alert on io-shop so its message describes the latency series it evaluates rather than an error rate. Evaluate tail latency over a shorter window so a slowdown pages near its onset.
Send feature-flag changes into the production change-event feed with accurate timestamps, so incident investigation sees them next to deploys and releases.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers saw slow account pages from {began} to {recovered}. The paging series rose from {series_before} before the onset to {series_while_broken} on average, peaking at {series_at_worst}. Failed requests did not rise above the usual noise ({errors_before} before, {errors_while_broken} during), so the harm was latency, not errors.

The latency rise started at the same time the monthly-spend-feature flag went from mostly off to fully on. Flag evaluations read 'off' for most requests at 07:58 and 'on' for every request from 07:59. No deploy or release was recorded in the window.

The newly enabled feature path was the best-supported cause of the extra tail latency on account pages. The Investigator suspects it reads purchase history directly instead of using the optional summary cache. Reverting the flag took the service back to baseline, which supports the flag as the cause, but the exact slow code path was not observed.

The flag was ramped to all traffic with nothing to check latency or stop the ramp, so the slow path reached every account-page request. The record does not show why the feature was enabled without a latency check. A draft fix is proposed.

contributing_factors.factor: The flag ramped from mostly off to fully on within about a minute with no staged rollout and no automatic latency guard, so a slow code path reached all account-page traffic.
The feature path appears not to use the summary cache, so its cost was not covered by the existing design. The proposed fix is still an unmerged draft.

The page came only at {alert_raised}, after the onset at {began}. The alert is named for latency but its text reports an error rate, which did not rise. Detection was slow and its description misleading.

The change-event feed returned no changes, so the flag toggle was invisible to the Investigator's change lookup. It was found only through the flag provider's history, and its recorded time did not match the log evidence.

input.executive_summary: For about {duration}, from {began} to {recovered}, some shoppers on io-shop saw slow account pages. Slow responses are what the latency series measured: it averaged {series_while_broken} during the incident against {series_before} before, and peaked at {series_at_worst}. The share of failed requests did not rise ({errors_before} before, {errors_while_broken} during), so pages were slow rather than broken. The slowdown began when a new account-page feature, the monthly spend feature, was switched on for all traffic. Argus identified the flag as the leading cause, switched it off, and watched the service return to baseline. The incident was held for {held}. A draft pull request with a proposed fix is awaiting review.

got_lucky: Only the slow tail of requests was affected and failures did not rise, so the harm was limited to slow pages for a short time.

The metrics show recovery at {recovered}, around the time the flag was reverted. The recovery may have been partly independent of the revert, so the flag's role rests mainly on the timing of the rollout.
went_well: Argus picked up the alert within a second and placed the onset correctly from the metrics.
Argus found the flag change through the flag provider's history even though the change-event feed was empty, and reverted it quickly.
The revert was checked against the service's metrics before the incident was closed, and a draft fix was proposed straight away.
went_wrong: Nothing guarded the flag rollout, so a latency regression reached all traffic.
The alert fired only after the onset, and its wording did not match what it measured.
The flag toggle did not appear in the change-event feed, and its recorded time disagreed with the logs.

input.root_cause: The monthly-spend-feature flag was ramped to fully on at the onset, and the code path it enables adds severe tail latency to some account-page requests. The likely reason is that it reads purchase history directly instead of using the optional summary cache. That mechanism is inferred, not confirmed, and the flag was not guarded by any latency check before or during its rollout.
input.symptom: Account pages were slow for some shoppers
